pages.text:
*Rule 18 of the Library at the Bottom of the Sea: Read it anyway.*

"The deep carries every sound," Wren said. She sat on the edge of the Returns Desk, her yellow boots dangling over the water. The thought bloomed in her mind like a sudden bubble, rising fast and bright. If the sea carried sound down to the lanterns, then a voice on the shore would carry it all the way down to the bottom.

Ravi frowned and tapped his knee in a nervous rhythm. "The water is thick," he said, trying to be helpful. "It absorbs noise. That is how we know the sea is quiet."

"Only if it is quiet," Wren replied. "But what if it is listening?"

She looked at Ottoline. The octopus tilted her head, her pince-nez sliding down her snout. One arm reached out to gently tap the water near Wren's boot. A small ripple spread, carrying the sound of the tap down into the dark.

"Rule Six," Ottoline said, her voice soft and rolling. "The deep carries every sound. Even the ones that are small. Even the ones that are afraid. The water does not forget a voice. It keeps it until someone is ready to hear it."

Wren looked at Ravi. "Forty children," she said. "That is not a whisper. That is a wave."

Ravi stared. His fingers stopped tapping. For the first time in his life, he did not have a number to count. He only had a feeling, big and heavy and warm, sitting in his chest.
pages.image: Wren, a ten-year-old girl in a coral-red sweater and yellow boots, sits on a stone desk in an underwater library, looking at Ravi, a boy in a striped shirt, while a large purple octopus with spectacles taps the water near her boot.

pages.text:
Back on the surface, the attic room held the scent of salt and old paper. Wren spread a long sheet of white paper on the floor; it was not fancy, just the kind Mrs. Pell used for wrapping returns, soft and slightly crumpled from handling.

Ravi produced a list, written in his neat, tight handwriting. "Room 4. Ms. Alvarez. The fishermen at the dock. The baker. The boy who lives next to the lighthouse." He looked at the list, then at Wren. "We need to tell them."

"We don't need to tell them," Wren said. She picked up a pencil, a stubby one worn down to a point like a crayon she had already finished. "We need to invite them."

She wrote one line in the center of the paper. Her letters were wobbly, but they were hers. *Bring a book. Bring your voice. Low tide, sunrise, the Saltmarrow Light.*

Ravi stared at the words. He had never written an invitation before, only lists, checking boxes and counting pages. He looked at the attic door, then at the paper.

"It is very simple," he said.

"Yes," Wren said. "That is the point."

Ravi picked up the pencil. He did not add anything, just holding it and feeling the quiet promise of the invitation rest in his hand.
pages.image: Wren and Ravi sit on the floor of a cozy attic room, working on a large sheet of white paper with a pencil; Wren has short black curls and a coral-red sweater, Ravi has a side part and a striped shirt.

pages.text:
Squib arrived hovering in the air, his teal skin flickering with gold speckles of excitement. He held out a small, smooth shell sealed with a message, extending a single careful arm to offer it to Wren.

"From the head librarian," Squib said, his voice squeaking like a rusty hinge. "She says the whole Library will be listening. Every arm. Every heart. Even the slow ones."

Wren took the shell, feeling its warmth against her palm, and broke the seal. Inside lay a tiny scrap of paper folded small as a petal, covered in handwriting that was elegant, looping, and precise.

*We shall be delighted. Please do not chase any words.*

Wren laughed, a sound rising from deep in her belly where the funny parts of stories live. She held the note up for Ravi to see.

"She is teasing us," Ravi said, though a small, shy smile pushed through his expression.

Squib shifted to a soft, happy pink. "I am very proud," he admitted. "And also slightly terrified. Do you think the lanterns will break?"

"No," Wren said. "They will glow."
pages.image: A small teal cuttlefish with wavy eyes holds out a white shell to Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls, while Ravi, a boy in a striped shirt, looks on with a smile in a dimly lit room.

pages.text:
Mrs. Pell stood in the center of the room, holding a brown box that looked as sturdy as her own back. It was full of books, and she was staring at the empty shelf where they had once lived with the quiet, serious face of a woman who has just finished a very long homework assignment.

"Mrs. Pell," Wren said, stepping closer. "Can we use the reading nook? Just for a minute? We need to plan something."

Mrs. Pell turned. Her eyes, behind their round tortoiseshell glasses, were kind but deeply tired, like a lamp that had been burning since dawn. She looked at the box in her hands, then at Wren.

"I am packing," she said.

"We know," Ravi said, refusing to look away, though his hands were tucked firmly into the pockets of his khaki shorts. "But the library is not just the books. It is the people who read them."

Mrs. Pell was silent for a long time. Dust motes drifted through the afternoon light from the high windows, swirling slowly like flour in the air. She set the box down on the floor. It made a soft, heavy thud that seemed to settle the room.

Then she reached out and unfastened the flap. She pulled out a single book, a hardcover with a cracked cover, and held it against her chest.

"Dear," she said, her voice thin and bright as a bell. "I have waited a long time for someone to ask me to open a door."
pages.image: Mrs. Pell, an elderly woman with white curls and glasses, stands in a library holding a brown box, looking at Wren and Ravi who stand near the reading nook, with sunlight streaming through the windows.

pages.text:
Dad was standing on the dock, checking the ropes on the *Gull*, his green wool cap tilted to one side. He looked up when Wren walked onto the planks, his beard messy with salt air.

"Dad," Wren said. "I need the ferry lantern. And the foghorn."

He looked at her. He did not ask why, just nodded. "The foghorn wakes the whole bay," he said. "And the lantern... that is a special light."

"It is perfect," Wren said.

That night, Wren lay in bed and looked at the tide table on the wall. The numbers were small and black, but they were clear. The lowest tide of the summer was tomorrow morning, right at dawn.

Her stomach flipped, a cold, sharp feeling like swallowing an ice cube. But underneath the fear, there was something else, something warm and rising.

She took a deep breath. The sea outside her window was dark and quiet.

"Right," she whispered to the moon. "One page."
pages.image: Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls, lies in bed looking up at a tide chart on the wall, with a view of the night sea and a lighthouse beam through the window.
